sections.heading: What are Web Robots?
sections.content: Web robots (also called crawlers or spiders) are automated programs that fetch pages on the Internet. Indexing robots collect content for search engines; other agents monitor sites, check links, or perform specialized tasks. This lesson covers how robots discover and crawl pages and how site owners can guide their behavior.

definitions.definition: Automated agent that fetches web pages following links and rules.
A program acting on behalf of a user; robots are a type of agent.
A system that uses crawlers to index content and answer queries.
Historic terms for exploratory agents; not typical for modern search crawling.

sections.heading: How robots decide where to go
content: Seeds: starting URLs provided by the search engine or system.
Link discovery: following hyperlinks found in pages.
Sitemaps: XML sitemaps published by sites help discovery.
Re‑crawling: scheduling based on change frequency and importance.

sections.heading: Robots Exclusion Standard (robots.txt)
sections.content: Websites can provide a /robots.txt file at the root (e.g., https://example.com/robots.txt) to communicate crawl directives. Typical fields: User-agent, Disallow, Allow. Not all robots comply; reputable crawlers respect it. The file is public, so do not list sensitive paths you wish to keep secret.

sections.heading: robots.txt examples
sections.content:
# Block everything for one agent
User-agent: BadBot
Disallow: /

# Allow all agents except admin area
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Allow: /

# Point to sitemap
Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml

sections.heading: Meta Robots and rel attributes
sections.content: Per‑page controls can be set via HTML meta robots tags or HTTP headers (e.g., noindex, nofollow) and via link attributes such as rel="nofollow". These are honored by most search engines for indexing choices.

sections.heading: Operational considerations for admins
content: Monitor server logs to distinguish bots from users.
Rate limiting / crawl rate: some crawlers honor settings in webmaster tools; robots.txt has no standard 'crawl-delay' (some robots use it, but it's not universal).
Disallow confidential endpoints and use proper auth; robots.txt is advisory, not a security mechanism.
Publish sitemaps to improve discovery of canonical URLs.

sections.heading: Hands‑on: design a robots.txt
sections.description: Draft rules for a site that blocks /private/, allows everything else, and exposes a sitemap.
steps: Write a robots.txt that disallows /private/ for all agents.
Add a Sitemap directive pointing to https://your-site.example/sitemap.xml.
Explain why robots.txt should not list secrets and how to protect content properly.

quiz.question: Where must robots.txt be located to be effective?

options.a: Any folder, crawlers scan them all

quiz.question: What does Disallow: / in robots.txt for an agent mean?

options.b: Block the whole site for that agent
options.c: Index but do not follow links

quiz.question: Which statement is TRUE about robots.txt?

options.a: It is a strict security control enforced by browsers
options.b: It is advisory; reputable crawlers comply, but it is public and not a secret keeper
options.c: It hides files from all users if Disallow is present

quiz.question: Which meta setting prevents a page from appearing in search results?
What is a practical way to improve discovery of pages you want indexed?

options.a: List them in robots.txt under Disallow
options.b: Publish an XML sitemap and link them internally
